reception.text: The Associated Press carried the full text from Buffalo the night it was issued, and papers printed it the next morning.
reception.source: San Francisco Call, September 15, 1901, p. 13 (Associated Press); New-York Tribune, September 15, 1901

reception.text: At half past three on the day of mourning, New York's trolleys, elevated trains, power-house dynamos and harbor boats stopped for five minutes while crowds stood bareheaded.
Telegraph operators across the country paused for the same five minutes.
In Washington, services were held in nearly every church, and stores and businesses closed.
Westminster Abbey held a service by command of King Edward, and most business houses in Manila closed.

No organized objection to the proclamation's call to worship has been found in the period press, but the leading church-and-state weekly was out of print and the anarchist press had been shut down, so the silence is weak evidence.

political_impact.text: Before the oath, Roosevelt pledged to continue McKinley's policy "absolutely unbroken," and the mourning proclamation served as the ceremonial side of that same reassurance.
After the oath, Roosevelt asked McKinley's Cabinet to stay in office, keeping John Hay as Secretary of State until Hay's death in 1905.
The appointed day ended a five-day national funeral, with ceremonies under the Capitol dome on September 17 and the Canton service on September 19.
At Canton, McKinley's body was placed in the Werts Receiving Vault at West Lawn Cemetery under Army guard rather than buried.
Abraham Isaak, editor of the anarchist paper Free Society in Chicago, was arrested with his family within two days of the shooting, and police destroyed his presses.

legacy.text: McKinley was entombed in the McKinley National Memorial in Canton in 1907, and Roosevelt gave the oration at its dedication.
The 1903 immigration act barred anarchists and opponents of all organized government from entering the country and from naturalization.
legacy.source: Act of March 3, 1903, ch. 1012, 32 Stat. 1213, secs. 2, 38, 39

legacy.text: Congress first funded Secret Service protection of the President in 1906 and first authorized it by statute in 1913; permanent authorization came in 1951.
When Roosevelt died in 1919, the proclamation announcing his death used the narrower form for former Presidents: flags at half staff and military honors, with no day of mourning or prayer.

later_actions.text: Congress added anarchists to the classes barred from entering the United States.
Congress first appropriated money for protecting the person of the President.
Congress first authorized Secret Service protection of the President by statute.
President Wilson proclaimed the death of ex-President Roosevelt, ordering flags at half staff for thirty days.
Congress met in joint session to hear Henry Cabot Lodge eulogize Roosevelt.

uncertain: The hour Roosevelt signed the proclamation is not known.
How Hay's countersignature and the Great Seal were applied while Roosevelt was in Buffalo is not known; a seal warrant described by an auction house has not been located or examined.
Whose handwriting is on the Library of Congress draft, and whether it is the draft Ansley Wilcox rescued from the wastebasket, are not known.
